periods.activity_title: Reading Aloud and First Response to the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.220): pre-reading discussion — why words matter, non-verbal communication
Reading for Appreciation (p.223): rhyming words and ABAB rhyme scheme identification

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading prompt from Reflect and Respond: students share briefly why words matter and whether communication is possible without them. Take two or three quick responses to activate prior thinking.
Teacher reads the poem aloud, with students following in their textbooks (p.220–221). Read each stanza with deliberate pacing; pause after each stanza to let the imagery settle before moving on.
Students read the poem a second time silently, then in pairs identify four sets of rhyming words and note the ABAB pattern for each stanza, drawing from Reading for Appreciation (p.223).
Pairs share their rhyme-scheme findings with the class; teacher confirms the ABAB pattern and draws attention to how the regular metre gives the poem its hymn-like quality.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem for the first time, students should notice that every stanza closes with a diminishing or ironic note about words — this is the poem's emotional engine. A common pitfall is treating 'ABAB' as a naming exercise rather than noticing how the alternating rhyme creates a sense of balance and then disappointment. Students who have not yet found the contrast between stanzas 1 and 4 (both opening with 'if words could') can be asked to compare those two openings.

periods.activity_title: Poetic Devices and Critical Reflection on Extracts

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.223): identify poetic device and poet's intent in phrases (i)–(iv)
Critical Reflection (p.224): five questions on Extract 1 — pilgrim metaphor, heart's need, words as weeds

homework.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.223): identify poetic device and intent in phrases (v)–(vii)

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the rhyme scheme and the poem's central paradox — abundant words, empty effect — established in the reading aloud, before moving into device analysis.

Students work in pairs on phrases (i)–(iv) from Reading for Appreciation (p.223): identify the device (simile, metaphor, simile, hyperbole respectively) and articulate what each communicates about the inadequacy of hollow speech. Pairs share findings; teacher consolidates on the board.

Teacher leads a whole-class close-reading of Extract 1 from Critical Reflection (p.224): the pilgrim metaphor, when the heart 'needs' words, the weeds comparison, two emotions of the heart, and the broader claim about communication. Students write answers in their notebooks; teacher circulates and addresses misconceptions.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem and identified its rhyme scheme, students are now ready to work at the level of individual images. The common pitfall with the pilgrim metaphor is paraphrasing it rather than explaining why 'pilgrim' — the idea of restless, purposeful, yet homeless searching — is a precise choice for a heart that language fails. Students who conflate simile and metaphor should be redirected: 'words like summer birds' uses 'like' explicitly, whereas 'heart, a pilgrim' omits it. Phrases (v)–(vii) are set as self-study for students to complete independently.

periods.activity_title: Exclamation Marks, Hyperbole, and Figurative Phrase Matching

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.223): MCQ — emotions conveyed by exclamation marks in stanzas 4, 5, 6
Check Your Understanding (p.223–224): hyperbole identification and paired completion exercise
Vocabulary in Context (p.226): match figurative phrases to meanings, then use each in a sentence

time_bands.activity: Students individually answer the exclamation-mark MCQ from Check Your Understanding (p.223), then discuss in pairs the emotions behind stanzas 4, 5, and 6 — admiration, frustration, disillusionment — before teacher confirms the correct option and explains how punctuation signals tone.

Teacher introduces hyperbole using the feast line from the poem; students work in pairs to complete the four hyperbole sentences from Check Your Understanding (p.223–224), choosing the more exaggerated option in each case and explaining their choice.

Students individually complete the figurative-phrase matching from Vocabulary in Context (p.226) — six phrases paired with meanings — then write one original sentence for each phrase. Teacher reviews matches as a class and discusses how each phrase functions within the poem's argument about hollow versus sincere speech.

periods.teacher_notes: Having analysed poetic devices in the previous unit on phrases (i)–(iv), students now link punctuation choices to the poem's emotional arc. The common pitfall with the exclamation-mark question is assigning 'admiration' to stanza 4, because 'dear' sounds positive — clarify that the exclamation expresses tender wonder, not conventional admiration, and that the broader stanza is still ironic about words. The matching task in Vocabulary in Context is an opportunity to reinforce that the poem's figurative language is not decorative but argumentative: each phrase carries part of Swain's central claim.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Dialogue, Then Speaking on a Chosen Quotation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.227): mark four true statements from six about the Sonali–Vivek dialogue
Speaking Activity (p.228): select a quotation, explain it, share personal connection using verbal cues

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Sonali–Vivek transcript aloud at a natural pace while students listen and mark statements 1–6 from Listen and Respond (p.227) as true or false. After a second reading students finalise their four true statements and class checks answers together.

Teacher introduces the quotations on the board and models the speaking task structure: opening with a verbal cue ('I chose ___ because…'), explaining the quotation's meaning, then connecting it to a personal experience. Students have a brief preparation window to choose their quotation and organise their thoughts.

Selected students deliver their oral presentations from Speaking Activity (p.228), each using at least one verbal cue from the list. After each presentation, two classmates offer a short response — agreeing, disagreeing, or extending the idea — to keep the exchange dialogic.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript centres on the same theme as the poem — effective versus hollow communication — so the transition between the two tasks is thematically natural. Students often struggle with statement 5, which asserts that body language plays an insignificant role; the transcript directly contradicts this, so prompt students to listen for Sonali's explicit claim. In the speaking task, discourage students from simply reading a summary of the quotation; the verbal cues are scaffolds for genuine explanation and personal connection.
materials: Printed or board-displayed list of eight quotations

periods.activity_title: Essay Writing on a Quotation, then Non-Verbal Communication Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.229): plan and draft a five-paragraph argumentative essay on a chosen quotation
Learning Beyond the Text (p.230): read about Charles-Michel de l'Épée and discuss sign language as non-verbal communication

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.230): play the Non-verbal game in groups of six at home or free period

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the five-paragraph essay structure from Writing Task (p.229) on the board: introduction with quotation and thesis, two body paragraphs each with a topic sentence and evidence, one counterargument paragraph, and a conclusion. Students identify which quotation they will write on.

Students plan their essay using a brief outline (introduction claim, two evidence points, counterargument and refutation, conclusion) then draft all five paragraphs in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting students who stall on the counterargument to think of the most obvious objection to their claim.

Students exchange drafts with a partner for a quick peer-response pass: partner marks one strong sentence and one place where the reasoning could be sharper. Students make one revision based on the feedback before the unit closes.

Teacher introduces the brief passage on Charles-Michel de l'Épée from Learning Beyond the Text (p.230) and leads a whole-class discussion: what makes sign language a complete communication system, how it relates to the poem's argument that sincerity and form matter more than volume of words.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the poem's central claim — that few sincere words outweigh many hollow ones — students now extend that claim into formal argumentative writing. The most common drafting difficulty is the counterargument paragraph; students benefit from the prompt 'What would someone who disagrees with your quotation say, and why are they wrong?' The de l'Épée discussion anchors the beyond-text material in the poem's theme of non-verbal versus verbal communication, so the two halves of the unit share an intellectual thread rather than feeling separate.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, figurative imagery, and thematic argument using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Charles Swain's meditation on hollow versus sincere words, using simile, metaphor, and hyperbole across six stanzas.
items.item_stem: In the poem, Charles Swain compares words to summer birds. Which statement best explains what this comparison communicates about the nature of words?

options.label: A
options.text: Words are as free and unpredictable as wild birds.

options.label: B
options.text: Words are colourful and beautiful, like birds in summer.

options.label: C
options.text: Words arrive and depart quickly, leaving no lasting comfort behind.

options.label: D
options.text: Words bring warmth and brightness to a listener's heart.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student focuses on surface attractiveness of birds rather than their departure and the emptiness left behind.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses the warmth associated with birds with the poem's ironic point that words fail to provide warmth.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student picks up on the transience idea but misses the specific emotional claim — hollow words leave nothing, not just something unpredictable.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, figurative imagery, and thematic argument using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Charles Swain's meditation on hollow versus sincere words, using simile, metaphor, and hyperbole across six stanzas.
items.item_stem:
Read the second stanza on p.221, beginning “The heart, a pilgrim upon earth.”

1. Identify the poetic device used in the phrase “the heart, a pilgrim upon earth” and explain why the word ‘pilgrim’ is a precise choice for the heart in this context.
2. In the same stanza, words are compared to weeds. Analyse what this second comparison adds to Swain’s argument that goes beyond the summer-birds simile in the opening stanza.
3. Together, these two devices — the pilgrim metaphor and the weeds simile — suggest something about the relationship between emotional need and language. What is that suggestion, and how effectively does Swain use contrast across the two images to make his point?
items.visual_stimulus: Read the second stanza on p.221, beginning “The heart, a pilgrim upon earth.”

expected_elements: Metaphor identified; pilgrim captures restless, purposeful searching without rest.
Weeds simile: words are not merely absent but actively unwanted, cluttering rather than comforting.
Birds simile shows departure; weeds simile shows persistent worthlessness — escalation of inadequacy.
Together the images argue the heart’s need makes language’s failure feel worse, not neutral.
Credit evaluation of how effectively contrast across stanzas builds Swain’s cumulative argument.

items.source_lo: Student identifies specific information and evaluates claims about communication by listening to a dialogue.
items.source_context: Sonali and Vivek's conversation about effective communication, vocabulary, grammar, and body language for a declamation contest.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Sonali and Vivek. Decide whether each statement below is True or False.

1. Vivek mentions an inter-school declamation contest on the role of the English language in communication.
2. Sonali says she registered for the contest after Vivek told her about it.
3. According to Sonali, effective communication requires choosing words carefully and organising thoughts.
4. Vivek already knew that gestures and postures form part of communication before Sonali explained it.

options.text: According to Sonali, effective communication requires choosing words carefully and organising thoughts.
Sonali says she registered for the contest after Vivek told her about it.
Vivek already knew that gestures and postures form part of communication before Sonali explained it.
Vivek mentions an inter-school declamation contest on the role of the English language in communication.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — Vivek raises the contest topic. 2. False — Sonali says she registered early, not prompted by Vivek. 3. True — Sonali and Vivek together articulate this point. 4. False — Vivek asks Sonali how body language works, showing he was unaware.

items.source_lo: Student identifies specific information and evaluates claims about communication by listening to a dialogue.
items.source_context: Sonali and Vivek's conversation about effective communication, vocabulary, grammar, and body language for a declamation contest.
items.item_stem: In the conversation, Sonali explains why many people struggle to communicate effectively in English and then recommends a course of action. In two to three sentences, summarise her diagnosis of the problem and the solution she proposes, and then give one reason from the conversation that explains why body language is included in her solution.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sonali diagnoses the problem as insufficient vocabulary and grammar knowledge, which causes hesitation especially for non-native English speakers. She recommends building vocabulary and grammar to communicate with confidence. She includes body language because, as she explains, communication happens not only through words but also through gestures and postures, so both verbal and non-verbal channels must be developed.

items.item_stem: Describe, in two to three spoken sentences, the quotation on words or communication that you chose and explain in your own words what it means. Use one of the verbal cues provided: 'I chose ___ because…', 'I selected ___ since…', or 'I decided on ___ due to…'

expected_elements: Names the quotation and its author clearly.
Explains the quotation's meaning in own words, not by reading it.

items.source_context: Selecting and explaining a quotation on words and communication from a set including Swami Vivekananda and Emily Dickinson.
items.item_stem: Charles Swain's poem argues that a few sincere words are more valuable than many hollow ones. Do you agree or disagree? Present your argument in a short spoken response of four to five sentences, giving at least one reason with evidence from your own experience or observation, and acknowledge a possible opposing view before restating your position.

expected_elements: States a clear position — agreement or disagreement — at the outset.
Supports the position with a personal experience or observed example.
Acknowledges the opposing view before returning to their claim.
Closes with a restatement of position, not just a summary.
Maintains coherent argument structure and appropriate register throughout.

items.item_stem: A community notice board displays the message: 'Speak less, mean more.' Write a short notice (80–100 words) for your school newsletter announcing an inter-class debate on this statement. Include the motion, date, venue, and an invitation to participants.

expected_elements: Uses correct notice format: heading, date, venue, and issuing authority.
States the debate motion clearly and accurately.
Invites participation in a formal, courteous tone.
Stays within the 80–100 word limit with no irrelevant detail.

items.source_context: An essay exploring the value of mindful and meaningful speech, inspired by the poem's theme of quality over quantity.
items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of your school magazine (150–180 words) arguing that students should be encouraged to practise mindful speaking — choosing words with care and sincerity — rather than rewarding those who speak the most in class. Your letter must: state your argument clearly in the opening paragraph; support it with at least two specific reasons or examples; address one likely objection; and close with a call to action for the school.

expected_elements: Uses formal letter-to-editor format with sender address, date, and salutation.
Opens with a clear, arguable claim about mindful speaking in school.
Provides two distinct reasons or examples supporting the claim.
Acknowledges and refutes one plausible counterargument.
Closes with a specific, actionable recommendation for the school.

items.source_context: Six figurative phrases from the poem — including 'hosts of words' and 'wins its sunny way' — matched to meanings and used in sentences.
items.item_stem: Match each figurative phrase from the poem in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A (Phrase) | Column B (Meaning) |
|---|---|
| hosts of words | cheerfully makes progress in a quiet way |
| wins its sunny way | fails to move or affect someone emotionally |
| never touch the heart | a vast, overwhelming quantity of speech |
| depart and leave but empty air | words that look impressive but produce nothing of value |
| plants that cannot grow fruit | disappear without leaving any lasting comfort |
| satisfy the heart | fulfil a deep emotional or spiritual need |

answer_key.right: a vast, overwhelming quantity of speech
cheerfully makes progress in a quiet way
fails to move or affect someone emotionally

answer_key.left: depart and leave but empty air
answer_key.right: disappear without leaving any lasting comfort
words that look impressive but produce nothing of value
fulfil a deep emotional or spiritual need

items.source_lo: Student interprets figurative phrases in context and uses them accurately in original sentences.
items.source_context: Six figurative phrases from the poem — including 'hosts of words' and 'wins its sunny way' — matched to meanings and used in sentences.
items.item_stem: Two of the poem's figurative phrases — 'hosts of words' and 'wins its sunny way' — carry meanings that depend heavily on connotation rather than literal sense. For each phrase: (a) write one original sentence that uses the phrase correctly in a new context, and (b) in one sentence explain why the phrase's connotative meaning is more powerful than a plain equivalent would be.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable responses will use each phrase in a fresh, contextually appropriate sentence and offer a brief but reasoned explanation of why the figurative phrasing carries emotional or persuasive weight that a plain synonym (e.g. 'many words' or 'progresses cheerfully') would lose. Full credit requires both parts for both phrases.

items.source_lo: Student evaluates non-verbal communication as a meaning-making system through cultural and historical exploration.
items.source_context: Charles-Michel de l'Épée's founding of sign language and deaf education as a model of communication beyond spoken words.
items.item_stem: Charles-Michel de l'Épée developed a systematic sign language in eighteenth-century France to enable deaf students to communicate and learn. In two to three sentences, explain what de l'Épée's work demonstrates about communication that connects to Charles Swain's argument in the poem that sincerity and form matter more than the volume of words spoken.

expected_elements: Names de l'Épée's contribution: systematic sign language for deaf communication.
Connects his work to the poem's claim that sincerity and precision outweigh quantity.
Explains that sign language conveys meaning without spoken words, proving non-verbal channels can be complete.
Makes the link explicit: fewer or no spoken words can carry more meaning than hollow speech.

items.source_lo: Student evaluates non-verbal communication as a meaning-making system through cultural and historical exploration.
items.source_context: Charles-Michel de l'Épée's founding of sign language and deaf education as a model of communication beyond spoken words.
items.item_stem: Design a brief project proposal (one paragraph, 100–120 words) for a school exhibition on non-verbal communication systems across cultures — for example, sign languages, drum languages, or gesture-based communication traditions. Your proposal must: name at least two communication systems you would feature; explain why each is a complete meaning-making system; and include one way your exhibition would help students connect this knowledge to Charles Swain's idea that sincere, purposeful communication matters more than volume.

expected_elements: Names at least two distinct non-verbal communication systems with brief identification.
Explains why each system is complete — capable of conveying nuanced meaning.
Proposes a concrete exhibition element or activity for student engagement.
Connects the exhibition's message to the poem's theme of purposeful communication.
Writes in a clear, organised proposal style within the word limit.
